components/c01.coreIdea: Route each request to a healthy backend using the cheapest layer that has the signal you need.
flowLabels: route by IP, path, or load

cards.title: L4 vs L7
cards.body: L4 is fast and connection-aware. L7 reads HTTP, terminates TLS, and routes by path, header, or cookie.

cards.title: Choose a backend
cards.body: Round robin is simple; least-connections adapts to long work; consistent hashing limits remapping.

cards.title: Stay healthy
cards.body: Probe proactively, observe live errors, drain bad nodes, and keep spare capacity for failover.

cards.title: Avoid hidden state
cards.body: Sticky sessions create skew and brittle failover. Prefer stateless servers plus shared session storage.

components/c01.tradeoff: More application awareness enables smarter routing, but costs CPU, latency, and operational complexity.

components/c02.coreIdea: Cache expensive reads close to demand, then make staleness and invalidation explicit design decisions.

cards.title: Read patterns
cards.body: Cache-aside is flexible; read-through centralizes misses. Always define TTL, ownership, and fallback.

cards.title: Write patterns
cards.body: Write-through favors consistency; write-back favors throughput but risks loss and reordering.

cards.title: Control pressure
cards.body: Use request coalescing, jittered TTLs, prewarming, and stale-while-revalidate against stampedes.

cards.title: Measure the cache
cards.body: Track hit ratio, eviction rate, hot keys, item age, origin load, and tail latency—not just capacity.

components/c02.tradeoff: Every cache trades freshness and complexity for latency and source-of-truth load reduction.

components/c03.coreIdea: Serve cacheable bytes from nearby edge points while protecting the origin and preserving safe invalidation.

cards.title: Populate
cards.body: Pull CDNs fetch on first miss; push workflows pre-position known assets. Most systems combine both.

cards.title: Control freshness
cards.body: Cache-Control, TTL, versioned URLs, purge APIs, and stale serving define the consistency contract.

cards.title: Protect origin
cards.body: An origin shield collapses duplicate misses and keeps global edge churn away from core services.

cards.title: Use the edge
cards.body: Terminate TLS, compress, resize media, filter abuse, and run small latency-sensitive functions near users.

components/c03.tradeoff: Longer edge caching improves latency and cost, but increases the blast radius and duration of stale content.

components/c04.coreIdea: Persist work between producers and consumers so each side can scale, fail, and recover independently.

cards.title: Pick semantics
cards.body: Queues distribute work; pub/sub fans events out. Logs retain ordered history for independent replay.

cards.title: Assume duplicates
cards.body: At-least-once delivery is practical. Make handlers idempotent with stable event and operation IDs.

cards.title: Bound failure
cards.body: Retry with backoff, cap attempts, quarantine poison messages in a DLQ, and expose lag and age.

cards.title: Apply backpressure
cards.body: Limit in-flight work, pause partitions, shed low-priority load, and scale from queue depth plus age.

components/c04.tradeoff: Asynchrony improves resilience and throughput, but gives up immediate completion and introduces lag, duplicates, and ordering work.

components/c05.coreIdea: Admit traffic at a controlled rate before scarce downstream resources become the bottleneck.

cards.title: Token bucket
cards.body: Tokens refill steadily and allow bounded bursts. Capacity sets burst size; refill rate sets sustained traffic.

cards.title: Window choices
cards.body: Fixed windows are cheap but bursty at boundaries. Sliding log is exact; sliding counter is a useful compromise.

cards.title: Distribute safely
cards.body: Use atomic Redis updates or local leases. Decide whether small over-admission during failure is acceptable.

cards.title: Be a good API
cards.body: Return 429 plus Retry-After and quota headers; distinguish user, token, IP, route, and tenant limits.

components/c05.tradeoff: Stricter global accuracy costs coordination and latency; local limits are faster but can overshoot the global quota.

components/c06.coreIdea: Combine a small set of proven primitives to place data, reduce work, coordinate ownership, and retry safely.

cards.title: Place data
cards.body: Consistent hashing limits movement; virtual nodes smooth imbalance; explicit sharding keeps boundaries visible.

cards.title: Skip needless work
cards.body: Bloom filters can prove absence cheaply. False positives are possible; false negatives are not.

cards.title: Coordinate
cards.body: Leaders serialize ownership. Quorums overlap replicas when R + W > N, subject to repair and clock realities.

cards.title: Retry safely
cards.body: Idempotency keys turn repeated operations into the same logical result and must outlive client retry windows.

components/c06.tradeoff: Primitives simplify one failure mode at a time; composing them creates new invariants that must be stated and tested.

components/c07.coreIdea: Choose an interface whose coupling, latency, evolution, and delivery semantics match the interaction.

cards.title: Match the style
cards.body: REST fits resources, gRPC fits typed internal calls, and GraphQL fits client-shaped reads with governance.

cards.title: Design retries
cards.body: Make safe operations idempotent; use idempotency keys for create or charge actions that clients may retry.

cards.title: Page stable data
cards.body: Offset is simple but drifts under writes. Cursor pagination anchors continuation to a stable sort key.

cards.title: Push intentionally
cards.body: Webhooks fit server callbacks, SSE fits one-way streams, and WebSockets fit bidirectional low-latency sessions.

components/c07.tradeoff: A richer API reduces client round trips but increases server complexity, coupling, observability, and abuse surface.

ddia/ch01.coreIdea: Evaluate every data system through reliability, scalability, and maintainability—not a single peak-throughput number.

cards.title: Reliability
cards.body: Prevent component faults from becoming service failures; expect hardware, software, and human faults.

cards.title: Scalability
cards.body: Name the load parameter, observe how performance changes, then specify resources needed to hold an SLO.

cards.title: Tail latency
cards.body: Averages hide the users who wait. Percentiles expose queues, fan-out amplification, and the real experience.

cards.title: Maintainability
cards.body: Optimize for operability, simplicity, and evolvability so the system remains changeable after launch.

ddia/ch01.tradeoff: Optimizing one pillar can harm another; make the workload and service objective explicit before choosing architecture.

ddia/ch02.coreIdea: A data model shapes both how an application thinks and which queries and evolutions remain easy.

cards.title: Relational
cards.body: Strong joins and normalized many-to-many data; schema-on-write makes structure explicit before storage.

cards.title: Document
cards.body: Natural aggregates and locality; schema-on-read eases variation but references and joins can become awkward.

cards.title: Graph
cards.body: Vertices and edges make many-to-many traversal first-class when relationship shape is the central query.

cards.title: Declarative queries
cards.body: State what results you want and let the optimizer choose execution, parallelism, and access paths.

ddia/ch02.tradeoff: Choose for the dominant relationships and access patterns; no model removes impedance mismatch for every workload.

ddia/ch03.coreIdea: Storage engines turn writes into durable structures and indexes into read speed—at a measurable amplification cost.

cards.title: LSM trees
cards.body: Sequential writes and background compaction favor write throughput; reads consult multiple sorted levels.

cards.title: B-trees
cards.body: Fixed pages and in-place updates give predictable indexed reads, protected by a write-ahead log.

cards.title: Indexes
cards.body: Primary, secondary, clustered, covering, and multi-column indexes trade storage and write cost for query speed.

cards.title: OLTP vs OLAP
cards.body: Row stores serve selective transactions; columnar warehouses compress and scan analytical dimensions efficiently.

ddia/ch03.tradeoff: Every index accelerates a read path by adding write amplification, storage overhead, and maintenance work.

ddia/ch04.coreIdea: Evolve data safely by defining what old and new readers and writers must understand during mixed-version operation.

cards.title: Compatibility
cards.body: Backward: new code reads old data. Forward: old code reads new data. Rolling deploys usually need both.

cards.title: Formats
cards.body: Protobuf and Thrift use tagged fields; Avro resolves writer and reader schemas without field tags.

cards.title: Dataflow
cards.body: Databases, service calls, and asynchronous messages retain different version mixes and upgrade windows.

cards.title: RPC reality
cards.body: A network call is not a local call: it can time out, duplicate, partially fail, reorder, and cross versions.

ddia/ch04.tradeoff: Strict schemas improve safety and tooling; looser evolution improves flexibility but shifts errors into runtime and consumers.

ddia/ch05.coreIdea: Replication copies data for availability and locality, then forces explicit choices about leaders, lag, and conflicts.

cards.title: Single leader
cards.body: Simple ordering and conflict avoidance; failover and asynchronous lag can lose acknowledged writes.

cards.title: Multi-leader
cards.body: Useful across regions or offline clients, but concurrent writes require conflict detection and resolution.

cards.title: Leaderless
cards.body: Clients or coordinators read and write quorums; sloppy quorums, repair, and hinted handoff sustain availability.

cards.title: Read guarantees
cards.body: Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, and consistent-prefix reads make lag tolerable for specific experiences.

ddia/ch05.tradeoff: Synchronous replication improves durability and freshness; asynchronous replication improves latency and availability.

ddia/ch06.coreIdea: Partition data to scale, while keeping placement discoverable and rebalancing bounded as nodes and load change.

cards.title: Range partition
cards.body: Efficient contiguous scans, but sequential or time-based keys can concentrate writes on one shard.

cards.title: Hash partition
cards.body: Spreads keys more evenly, but destroys range locality and cannot cure a single extremely hot key.

cards.title: Secondary indexes
cards.body: Document-local indexes write locally and scatter reads; term-local indexes scatter writes and focus reads.

cards.title: Rebalance + route
cards.body: Move bounded partitions, avoid modulo-N churn, and let clients discover owners through routing metadata.

ddia/ch06.tradeoff: Even distribution reduces hotspots; locality reduces scatter-gather and cross-partition coordination.

ddia/ch07.coreIdea: Transactions group reads and writes into a correctness boundary, but isolation determines which races are actually prevented.

cards.title: ACID
cards.body: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability are guarantees with product-specific strength—not one universal mode.

cards.title: Weak isolation
cards.body: Read committed and snapshot isolation prevent some anomalies but may allow lost updates or write skew.

cards.title: Serializable
cards.body: Use actual serial execution, two-phase locking, or serializable snapshot isolation to match a serial order.

cards.title: 2PL is not 2PC
cards.body: Two-phase locking provides isolation; two-phase commit coordinates atomic commit across participants.

ddia/ch07.tradeoff: Stronger isolation simplifies application correctness but may cost contention, aborts, latency, and availability.

ddia/ch08.coreIdea: Distributed systems live with partial failure: messages, clocks, and processes can fail independently and ambiguously.

cards.title: Timeouts are guesses
cards.body: Silence cannot distinguish a dead node, slow node, lost request, or lost response; tune against false suspicion.

cards.title: Clocks mislead
cards.body: Wall clocks jump; monotonic clocks measure duration. Clock confidence matters when ordering or expiring ownership.

cards.title: Pauses break leases
cards.body: A process can stop past its lease and resume unaware. Fencing tokens let storage reject stale owners.

cards.title: Choose a model
cards.body: Safety claims depend on synchrony assumptions, crash behavior, Byzantine behavior, and quorum membership.

ddia/ch08.tradeoff: Aggressive failure detection recovers faster but falsely ejects healthy slow nodes; patience preserves work but delays failover.

ddia/ch09.coreIdea: Consistency and consensus define which global facts processes can safely agree on despite faults and reordering.

cards.title: Two meanings
cards.body: Linearizability is a recency guarantee across objects; serializability is a transaction isolation guarantee.

cards.title: CAP boundary
cards.body: During a network partition, a linearizable service must choose between rejecting requests and risking divergence.

cards.title: Order precisely
cards.body: Causal order captures dependencies; total-order broadcast gives every node the same durable message sequence.

cards.title: Consensus
cards.body: Agreement, integrity, and termination underpin leader election, unique constraints, atomic broadcast, and membership.

ddia/ch09.tradeoff: Global ordering makes invariants easier to enforce, but coordination adds latency and can reduce availability during partitions.

ddia/ch10.coreIdea: Batch systems transform bounded immutable inputs through restartable stages into reproducible derived outputs.

cards.title: Unix model
cards.body: Small tools communicate through uniform byte streams; composition and immutability make pipelines understandable.

cards.title: MapReduce
cards.body: Mappers emit key-value pairs; shuffle groups keys; reducers process each key's complete value set.

cards.title: Joins
cards.body: Sort-merge and reduce-side joins move data by key; broadcast joins copy a small side to every worker.

cards.title: Dataflow engines
cards.body: DAG schedulers keep intermediates in memory, pipeline operators, and recompute lost partitions from lineage.

ddia/ch10.tradeoff: Materialized stages are slow but durable and inspectable; pipelined execution is fast but needs lineage-based recovery.

ddia/ch11.coreIdea: Stream processing treats unbounded events as data, maintaining derived views while handling time, replay, and delivery.

cards.title: Broker models
cards.body: AMQP assigns transient messages to consumers; log brokers retain partitioned history for replay.

cards.title: CDC + event sourcing
cards.body: CDC derives a change stream from database state; event sourcing makes domain events the source of truth.

cards.title: Time + windows
cards.body: Event time reflects reality; processing time reflects arrival. Watermarks bound how long to await late data.

cards.title: Exactly once
cards.body: Usually means effectively-once effects via checkpoints, transactions, idempotency, or deterministic replay.

ddia/ch11.tradeoff: Waiting longer improves event-time completeness; emitting earlier lowers latency but increases corrections and retractions.

ddia/ch12.coreIdea: Build data systems as composable sources and derived views, with end-to-end correctness spanning every boundary.

cards.title: Derived data
cards.body: Caches, indexes, warehouses, and models should be rebuildable from an authoritative durable source.

cards.title: Unbundled database
cards.body: Compose specialized storage and processing tools around a common log instead of forcing one system to do all jobs.

cards.title: End-to-end
cards.body: Exactly-once internals cannot guarantee user correctness without request IDs, constraints, audits, and outcome visibility.

cards.title: People matter
cards.body: Auditability, privacy, fairness, consent, and feedback loops are system properties—not post-launch add-ons.

ddia/ch12.tradeoff: Specialized components improve local fit but increase integration contracts, metadata, lineage, and operational responsibility.
